bio.en: Madhavan Ramanujam is one of the world's leading pricing and monetization strategists, a former managing partner at Simon-Kucher who has advised over 250 companies including 30 unicorns, author of Monetizing Innovation and its sequel Scaling Innovation, and now invests full-time in early-stage AI companies through his own fund.
bio.zh: Madhavan Ramanujam 是全球顶尖的定价与变现战略专家，曾任 Simon-Kucher 的管理合伙人，为包括 30 家独角兽在内的 250 多家公司提供顾问服务；他是《Monetizing Innovation》及其续作《Scaling Innovation》的作者，目前通过自己的基金全职投资早期 AI 公司。

summary.en: Madhavan argues that in the AI era, winners must master monetization from day one and resist anchoring customers on low price points like $20/month, because 20% of what you build drives 80% of willingness to pay. He introduces a simple two-by-two for picking a pricing model and explains why the coveted top-right quadrant is true outcome-based pricing, where you have both autonomy and attribution. The conversation covers how to gain pricing power, tactical negotiation advice, and the most common traps founders fall into that prevent durable, profitable businesses. He stresses that great founders must dominate both market share and wallet share—and that getting pricing right early is far cheaper than fixing it later.
summary.zh: Madhavan 认为，在 AI 时代，赢家必须从第一天起就精通变现，不能把客户锚定在每月 20 美元这样的低价上，因为你构建的东西里，有 20% 决定了 80% 的支付意愿。他介绍了一个用来选择定价模型的简单四象限，并解释了为什么大家都想要的那个右上角，是真正的“基于结果的定价”——既拥有自主权，又能清晰归因。对话涵盖了如何获得定价权、具体的谈判建议，以及创始人最常掉进去、导致无法建立持久盈利业务的那些陷阱。他强调，优秀的创始人必须同时拿下市场份额和钱包份额，而且尽早把定价做对，远比日后返工便宜得多。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: The good founders need to be able to dominate both market share and wallet share. It is not a choice. You need to get better at both.
turns.zh: 优秀的创始人需要能够主导市场份额和钱包份额。这不是一个选择。你需要在这两方面都变得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like every company wants to be an AI company these days. How is AI pricing different?

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: The winners in AI will need to master monetization from day one. If you're bringing a lot of value to the table and you start at training your customers to expect $20 a month and you anchored yourself on a low price point, you're in trouble. 20% of what you build drives 80% of the willingness to pay. But the irony is that that 20% is the easiest thing to build often.
turns.zh: 人工智能领域的赢家需要从第一天起就掌握盈利能力。如果你带来了很多价值，并且开始培训你的客户期望每月 20 美元，并且你将自己固定在低价点上，那么你就有麻烦了。你所构建的 20% 会驱动 80% 的支付意愿。但讽刺的是，这 20% 往往是最容易构建的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What would you say is the biggest lesson you want founders to take away?

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: If you think about market share and wallet share, let's think about it as a two-by-two. You see some who would say, "I'm going to monetize earlier on," but they might miss out on acquisition opportunities. And every chapter ends with how this particular strategy circumvents a single-engine problem and helps you focus on market share and wallet share at the same time. And there's also CEO questions and leadership questions that people should reflect on when they architect towards profitable growth and are they on the right track? I mean, think about this ways. If you're flying a aircraft, you don't want to flight on one engine. Why do you actually want to do that for your business?
turns.zh: 因此，如果我必须总结这本书的核心论点，基本上就是，如果你想建立一家持久的企业，你需要能够实现盈利增长。这意味着你需要能够掌握两个引擎：市场份额和钱包份额。 (00:07:26)：表面上听起来很简单，但实际上相当复杂。因为如果你把它解开，为了获得市场份额和钱包份额，你需要擅长获取、货币化和保留，比如获取客户，从他们身上赚到初始钱，而且还要持续赚钱，让你的客户真正推荐更多客户。 (00:07:46)：实际上，许多公司所做的就是专注于单一引擎策略。因此，他们只关注这两个主题之一，而几乎排除另一个主题。这会导致各种情况。你会看到公司说：“我将不惜一切代价实现增长并推迟货币化。”你会看到有些人会说，“我要早点赚钱”，但他们可能会错过收购机会。或者还有一些人过于专注于一小部分忠诚的客户群，以至于他们既没有货币化也没有真正获得客户。 (00:08:17)：所以优秀的创始人需要能够主导市场份额和钱包份额。这不是一个选择。你需要在这两方面都变得更好。但这并不意味着您在所有给定时间点都对市场份额和钱包份额投入同等的精力，而是意味着您对这两个主题给予同等的关注，并深思熟虑权衡，并说：“我如何才能真正同时考虑这两个主题，以便我的架构朝着盈利增长的方向发展？”这是本书的核心论点。 (00:08:47)：我们实际上展示了九种策略，这些策略实际上可以帮助公司实现盈利增长。每一章都以这种特定策略如何规避单引擎问题并帮助您同时关注市场份额和钱包份额作为结尾。人们在构建盈利增长目标时还应该反思首席执行官和领导力问题，他们是否走在正确的轨道上？我的意思是，想一想这个方法。如果您驾驶飞机，您不会想使用一台发动机飞行。为什么你真的想为你的企业这样做？

A market share that won, is different from a market share that is actually held. If you're so acquisition focused, you're actually focused on getting more and more customers, but you're not spending enough time with customers that you actually got to keep them, upsell them, keep them happy, et cetera. So you might fall into that trap. (00:10:34): If you're a moneymaker, you fall into one of two traps. The first one is you might nickel and dime your customers to death. Because you're focused on monetization, you might come up with a very differentiated pricing model, different levels, hidden fees, things to charge for many different things and come across as just trying to nickel and dime your customer. (00:10:53): The second trap that a moneymaker actually falls into is that you fall into the price premium paradox where you think that pricing high actually indicates value, but your price is so high that you actually start hurting your acquisition, so it just becomes irrelevant for most people. (00:11:13): If you're in the community builder, you actually fall into two common traps. The first one is you're focused so much on the foundation that you actually miss the frontier, which is you're so focused on your loyal customer base that you forget to attract different types of customers and you're not acquiring. (00:11:30): And the second trap that you fall into if you're a community builder is you train your customers to expect more for less. Because you're so eager to satisfy your loyal base, you start giving them more and more, and you're training your best customer base to expect more for less. (00:11:46): So these six traps are very common across these archetypes. Being a profitable growth architect means that you're avoiding these traps. In other words, you're simultaneously being a disruptor, a moneymaker, and a community builder all at the same time. And how do you actually have that archetype and the right strategies to actually go about your business?
turns.zh: 因此，让我们解开与原型相关的陷阱。如果您是颠覆者原型，您可能会陷入两个陷阱之一。第一个是你可能会落地，但你可能不会扩张。就像你渴望获得一样，你实际上可能已经以更少的代价放弃了很多，并且你已经放弃了农场，但你没有任何东西可以扩展。这是你可能掉入的第一个陷阱。 (00:10:12)：你实际上陷入的第二个陷阱是你开始...赢得的市场份额与实际持有的市场份额不同。如果你如此专注于获取客户，那么你实际上专注于获得越来越多的客户，但你没有花足够的时间与客户相处，以至于你实际上必须留住他们，向他们追加销售，让他们满意，等等。所以你可能会掉进这个陷阱。 (00:10:34)：如果你是一个赚钱者，你就会陷入两个陷阱之一。第一个是你可能会坑害你的客户。因为你专注于货币化，所以你可能会想出一个非常差异化的定价模式、不同的水平、隐藏费用、对许多不同的东西收取的费用，并且给人留下的印象只是想从你的客户那里赚点小钱。 (00:10:53)：赚钱者实际上陷入的第二个陷阱是，你陷入了价格溢价悖论，你认为高定价实际上表明了价值，但你的价格太高了，以至于你实际上开始损害你的收购，所以它对大多数人来说变得无关紧要。 (00:11:13)：如果您是社区建设者，您实际上会陷入两个常见的陷阱。第一个是你过于关注基础，以至于实际上错过了前沿，也就是说，你过于关注忠诚的客户群，以至于忘记了吸引不同类型的客户，而你却没有获得客户。 (00:11:30)：如果您是社区建设者，您会陷入的第二个陷阱是您训练客户以更少的成本获得更多的期望。因为您非常渴望满足您的忠实客户群，所以您开始为他们提供越来越多的服务，并且您正在训练您最好的客户群以更少的成本获得更多的回报。 (00:11:46)：所以这六个陷阱在这些原型中非常常见。成为一名盈利增长架构师意味着您要避免这些陷阱。换句话说，你同时是一个颠覆者、一个赚钱者和一个社区建设者。您如何真正拥有这种原型和正确的策略来实际开展您的业务？

turns.zh: 当然。因此，我将提出一些策略。也许我会采取的第一个是我们所说的“美丽简单的定价”。因此，在您的早期阶段，制定非常简单的定价并且不会在销售对话中造成太多摩擦是非常重要的。我的意思是，您可能应该在周一早上回去进行资产测试，让您的一些早期潜在客户或客户向您阐明定价策略，对吗？如果他们实际上代表您销售，他们会如何描述定价策略？如果他们不能以简单的方式结合上下文并进行实际解释，那么您就没有简单的定价策略。就这么简单。 (00:13:02)：拥有一个简单的定价策略也意味着你的定价需要能够讲述一个价值故事，因为你需要根据你实际带来的价值来确定你的价格。 (00:13:15)：超人就是一个很好的例子。当他们开始时，他们实际上是在与免费电子邮件产品竞争，并且他们正在提供优质的电子邮件体验。您实际上如何定价？我认为 Superhuman 的团队与 Rahul 和其他人做得非常好。他们提出了每月 30 美元的价格点，这非常简单。但他们讲述这个故事的方式是，你每天支付一美元，实际上可以在一周内获得四个小时的生产力，然后突然之间，定价看起来并不算太离谱。我的意思是，这就像一周内喝一杯拿铁咖啡实际上可以节省四个小时的价格。为什么我实际上不这样做，对吧？ (00:13:50)：定价情境化和价值故事并不需要只适用于优质产品。如果你再举个例子，像地铁 5 美元长的地铁是一种不同的方式来讲述定价故事，哦，只要 5 美元，你实际上会得到很多价值。如此精美简单的定价实际上意味着提出一个简单的定价策略，您的客户可以立即获得，而您的定价实际上讲述了一个价值故事，以及您如何真正获得它。因此，在本书中，我们列出了 10 个不同事项的清单，您实际上需要查看这些事项，以确保您的定价非常简单。

And so in the scale-up phase, I think one of the most important strategies is to master negotiations and really get better at acing negotiations, especially if you're in a B2B situation. And how do you actually do that? Because you need to be able to talk about the value and contextualize your price based on those kind of conversations. (00:15:25): So to master negotiations, it comes down to actually three things. Mastering gives and gets, being good at value selling, and third, having the right negotiation strategies. So let's unpack that each at a time. (00:15:39): So giving and getting, why is that important? Because in a negotiation, typically you're giving. I mean, you're giving concessions. People are asking. If you don't get anything back, you're basically indicating to the other person that they can keep beating you up and you need to keep giving. But if you're giving something but you ask for something in exchange, then you're basically bringing authenticity into the negotiation because it actually means something to you to give, so you're asking something back. It actually makes the negotiation way more effective. (00:16:10): And in the book we actually talk about the top 10 gets in B2B and the top 10 gets in B2C. One of my favorite gets in the B2B situation is what I call as conducting a value audit. So what this means is if you're giving a concession, ask for a value audit in exchange where every six months a team internally from your customers would be commissioned to actually conduct a value assessment of your products so that it becomes their business case and you co-create it with them saying how much value is actually produced. And this is great because if they actually engage in that, that gives you tremendous pricing power for renegotiations because it is their business case, they're championed it internally, and you're pretty much making your products pretty sticky. So it's a pretty harmless get, but it could be very powerful for future negotiations. So being good at-
turns.zh: 是的。美丽简单的定价就是启动。确切地。因此，在扩大规模阶段，我认为最重要的策略之一是掌握谈判并真正更好地进行谈判，尤其是在 B2B 情况下。你实际上是如何做到这一点的？因为您需要能够谈论价值并根据此类对话来确定您的价格。 (00:15:25)：因此，要掌握谈判，实际上可以归结为三件事。掌握给予和索取，善于价值销售，第三，制定正确的谈判策略。因此，让我们一次将其拆开。 (00:15:39)：那么给予和获得为什么那么重要？因为在谈判中，通常你是在给予。我的意思是，你在做出让步。人们在问。如果你没有得到任何回报，你基本上是在向对方表明，他们可以继续殴打你，而你需要继续付出。但如果你给予一些东西，但你要求一些东西作为交换，那么你基本上是在谈判中引入了真实性，因为这实际上对你来说意味着给予一些东西，所以你要求一些回报。它实际上使谈判方式更加有效。 (00:16:10)：在书中，我们实际上讨论了 B2B 领域的前 10 名和 B2C 领域的前 10 名。在 B2B 情况下，我最喜欢的做法之一就是进行价值审计。因此，这意味着，如果您做出让步，则要求进行价值审计，作为交换，每六个月，您的客户内部团队将被委托对您的产品进行实际价值评估，以便它成为他们的业务案例，然后您与他们共同创建它，说明实际产生了多少价值。这很棒，因为如果他们真的参与其中，这会给你巨大的重新谈判定价权，因为这是他们的商业案例，他们在内部支持它，并且你几乎可以让你的产品变得非常粘。因此，这是一次相当无害的交易，但对未来的谈判可能非常有力。所以擅长——

turns.en: That's really smart.

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: ... gives and gets is... Thank you. Being good at gives and gets is really critical. (00:17:07): The second thing in mastering negotiations is being good at value selling. And for being good at value selling, you need to do three things. First, you need to be able to create the needs. Second, you need to be able to create affirmation loops. And the third one is creating a good ROI model. And let's talk about each of those. So creating needs is very important because many founders show up and try to understand what are the needs of the customers. That's one way to look at it. But you need to be able to create needs rather than just discover them. (00:17:38): So for instance, if you're a marketing automation AI product and you save, let's say, three weeks of work that actually needs to be done to actually get stuff in a dashboard that can be analyzed by marketing managers, the way you create the need is ask about existing processes and say, "Okay, so just so I understand, all of this stuff actually takes you three weeks to put data together to actually have meaningful dashboards for your marketing managers to take action. What if that was available to you instantaneously?" Oh, you have now just created a need, right? So being in that mindset of creating a need as opposed to just discovering them. (00:18:17): The second thing is creating affirmation loops. And this is really important. I've seen a lot of founders get into negotiations. They're so eager to talk about their products. They keep talking about the products without any affirmation from the other side. You need to pause and create affirmation loops, things like, for instance, "Okay, so far, you've seen all of this. How does this actually play out in your company? Do you see it as valuable? What about this dashboard do you actually like?" (00:18:44): So when you ask these kind of questions and your customers are playing back the value that they actually see in your product, you're creating affirmation loops, which become tremendously useful when you start selling the product finally. Because if they've agreed that there's value that is being produced, then you also have a better commercial discussion. (00:19:03): And the third one is creating a good ROI model. And I see a lot of founders work on a POC. And after the POC's over, they'll show up with an ROI model and try to defend a price. You've already lost the battle. I mean, no one is going to believe an ROI model that you just cooked up. Everyone is going to challenge you on assumptions. (00:19:22): The right way to think about an ROI model is to actually co-create it with your customers from day one, which means agree and validate on the assumptions and the inputs. So like, "Hey, how long does this process take today? How many engineers are there?" So you create ask questions that are all inputs to an ROI model. And if you have done that process and the customer agrees on all the inputs, they're very unlikely to push back on the output of an ROI model. So a POC needs to be framed as the purpose of a POC is to build a business case, and we are going to co-create an ROI model with the customer as opposed to it being a tech and product functionality feature test and you show up with an ROI model. (00:20:06): And when you're building an ROI model, there are many buckets to focus on, but there are three that are very critical. The first one is, what are the incremental gains that you actually bring to the table based on KPIs and metrics that your customer is tracking? So this could be things like incremental revenue, reduction in churn. These are the immediate, tangible, clear impact to the business line based on the products that you actually bring to the table. (00:20:33): The second bucket is cost savings. Are you reducing headcount? Are you reducing license costs? What are the tangible cost savings? (00:20:41): And the third one, which is often overlooked, is opportunity cost. For instance, if you save 10 hours of time for a team, what do they actually do with that 10 hours? That can also be quantified. So when you put all of these three things together, you start building a proper ROI model that you can actually use in your value selling to defend the right price. (00:21:02): So we talked about three steps in mastering negotiations. The first one was gives and gets. The second one was getting better at value selling. The third one is actually getting better at even negotiations and what strategies would you actually use. And there are a couple of strategies that we have found to be really productive. (00:21:20): The first one is to show up with options. Many founders rush with one product and one price and say, "Okay, this is a hundred K product, and that's what we are trying to sell." Inevitably, what will happen is the immediate focus of the conversation will be on the price, and you're only talking about price. (00:21:39): But if you have options on the table, let's say if you have a good, better, best, if you're a hundred K product, a 200K and a 300K option, then you're not just talking price, you're talking value. Because if your customer is budget conscious, they'll say, "Hey, I like the hundred K price point, but I actually like the functionality in your 200K product." Then your immediate question is, what in the functionality do you actually like? Why is that beneficial for you? So you switch the conversation back to value as opposed to just talking about price. And we have seen that with these kind of conversations, you're by far more better off to actually land in a much better place than just showcasing one product and one price. (00:22:18): And showcasing options doesn't need to be just different products. It could even be a pricing model choice. And I'd probably give a simple hack that people can try on Monday morning. I was talking to this founder who said, "Hey, I think the budget is about 100K. That's what I believe from the key stakeholder, but my product really brings crazy value. I could even charge, let's say, a 500K for this product, but I don't have the courage to actually go and ask for a 500K price because I kind of know a hundred K is the budget. What should I do?" So for those kind of situations, actually show up with options in your pricing model. (00:22:58): So we coached him to go in with a hundred K, plus 10% on any incremental value that you bring, or it's a 500K fixed. So now this is actually a great situation in negotiation. Because if you're price sensitive, you're focused on the hundred K. It's a small fee to actually get started. But the conversation will gravitate towards, "What is that 10%? How do you measure value?" That's a great conversation to have because now you're talking about, "How you add value? Where's the value generation? What portion would you take?" (00:23:28): And you see one of two situations. Either the customer say, "That's great. You're putting skin in the game. Let's go with a hundred K and 10%," or, 80% of the situations, you might actually want to avoid the outcome-based pricing as a buyer, but you're not really fixated on the 500K at that point. It is the premium that you're actually paying for the certainty. So no one is focusing on the 5K because of the hundred K option on the table, and you just put a 500K and got the courage to do that. And in this specific situation, that 500K got negotiated to 400K, and they just 4X the deal compared to where they would be. So having options on the table when you negotiate is critical. (00:24:05): And there's also some tactics that we showcase in the book, like anchoring is important. If you start high, you'll also end up higher. And also tapering concessions. How do you give concessions? I mean, the worst negotiators will start by giving a small concession and then give a bit more when someone asks like... You might give a 5% discount, and the procurement guy says, "That's not enough." "Okay, I'll give you 10% more." "Okay, that's not enough." "I'll give you 15." What are you indicating to the other person? You're just basically indicating that I can keep beating you up and I can get more discounts. (00:24:35): The best negotiators who taper the concessions. So they would say, "I can give you 15%." "Okay, I need more." "I'll give you five." "I need more." "I'll give you two." So you're automatically indicating to the other person that the negotiation's actually ending. So how do you taper concessions also become important. (00:24:51): So when you put all of these three things together, if you master your gives and gets, you get better at value selling, and you use the right negotiation strategy, you can extract full value from every deal. That's probably way more important when you're at the scale-up phase.
turns.zh: ...给予和得到就是...谢谢。善于给予和索取确实至关重要。 (00:17:07)：掌握谈判的第二件事是善于价值销售。为了擅长价值销售，你需要做三件事。首先，您需要能够创造需求。其次，您需要能够创建肯定循环。第三个是创建良好的投资回报率模型。让我们逐一讨论一下。因此创造需求非常重要，因为许多创始人都会出现并试图了解客户的需求是什么。这是看待它的一种方式。但你需要能够创造需求，而不仅仅是发现需求。 模型的输入。如果您完成了该过程并且客户同意所有输入，他们就不太可能拒绝投资回报率模型的输出。因此，需要构建 POC，因为 POC 的目的是构建业务案例，我们将与客户共同创建 ROI 模型，而不是进行技术和产品功能特性测试，然后您会看到 ROI 模型。 (00:20:06)：当您构建投资回报率模型时，有很多方面需要关注，但有三个方面非常关键。第一个是，根据客户跟踪的 KPI 和指标，您实际带来的增量收益是多少？所以这可能是诸如增加收入、减少客户流失之类的事情。这些是根据您实际提供的产品对业务线产生的直接、切实、明显的影响。 (00:20:33)：第二个目标是节省成本。您要减少员工人数吗？您是否正在降低许可成本？有哪些切实的成本节省？ (00:20:41)：第三个经常被忽视的因素是机会成本。例如，如果您为一个团队节省 10 小时的时间，他们实际上用这 10 小时做什么？这也是可以量化的。因此，当您将这三件事放在一起时，您就开始构建适当的投资回报率模型，您可以在价值销售中实际使用该模型来捍卫正确的价格。 (00:21:02)：我们讨论了掌握谈判的三个步骤。第一个是给予和获得。第二个是在价值销售方面做得更好。第三个实际上是在甚至谈判方面变得更好以及你实际会使用什么策略。我们发现有一些非常有效的策略。 (00:21:20)：第一个是显示选项。许多创始人急于推出一种产品和一种价格，然后说：“好吧，这是一款 100K 的产品，这就是我们想要销售的产品。”不可避免地，谈话的直接焦点将集中在价格上，而你只谈论价格。 (00:21:39)：但是如果你有多种选择，比如说你有一个好、更好、最好的产品，如果你有 100 K 的产品、200K 和 300K 的选择，那么你就不仅仅是在谈论价格，而是在谈论价值。因为如果您的客户注重预算，他们会说：“嘿，我喜欢 100 K 的价格点，但实际上我喜欢你们 200K 产品的功能。”那么您直接的问题是，您真正喜欢哪些功能？为什么这对你有利？因此，您将话题转回价值，而不是仅仅谈论价格。我们已经看到，通过此类对话，您实际上可以更好地到达一个比仅仅展示一种产品和一种价格更好的地方。 (00:22:18)：展示选项并不需要只是不同的产品。它甚至可能是定价模型的选择。我可能会提供一个简单的技巧，人们可以在周一早上尝试。我和这位创始人交谈时，他说：“嘿，我认为预算约为 10 万。这是我从关键利益相关者那里得到的信念，但我的产品确实带来了疯狂的价值。我什至可以为这个产品收取 50 万的价格，但我没有勇气真正去要求 50 万的价格，因为我知道 100 万是预算。我该怎么办？”因此，对于这种情况，请在定价模型中实际显示选项。 (00:22:58)：所以我们指导他投入 100 K，再加上您带来的任何增量值的 10%，或者固定为 500K。所以现在这其实是一个谈判的大好局面。因为如果您对价格敏感，您就会专注于数百K。实际开始时只需支付少量费用。但谈话会倾向于这样的问题：“那 10% 是什么？你如何衡量价值？”这是一次很棒的对话，因为现在你谈论的是，“你如何增加价值？价值产生在哪里？你会拿走哪一部分？” (00:23:28)：您会看到两种情况之一。客户要么会说：“那太好了。你是在冒险。让我们以 100 K 和 10% 为标准吧”，或者，在 80% 的情况下，作为买家，你可能实际上希望避免基于结果的定价，但此时你并不真正关注 turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: So POCs, when we talk about POCs, many founders think about a POC as a proof of technical functionality, and is their product actually working in their customer environments. And they set up the expectation that we are saying, "Hey, we are going to put the product, and we're going to see if it actually works." And they would probably say, "Should I charge for a POC versus not?" And we'll unpack that in a bit, should you or should you not. (00:32:10): And that's actually a completely wrong way of framing it. The POC should be framed as the entire goal of the POC is to create a business case, period, full stop. It is not to demonstrate product functionality fit within your customer environment's ability to integrate. All of that stuff is a consequence of the business case. (00:32:30): So if you frame it this way is you can say, "Look, it is a 30-day pilot for co-creating an ROI model and building a business case along with their users. If we see value at the end of the 30 days based on the business case, we can get to commercial discussions." So that way you've actually not talked about your price. You're only focused on co-creating a business case with the customer. And based on the business case, you can actually come up with a proper commercial agreement. And if they see value, they're going to pay you for it. So thinking about the POCs in that kind of manner. (00:33:03): And the question that I often get asked is, "Should I charge for a POC?" And the answer is yes, but smartly. Let's talk about why it's important to charge. The reason you need to charge for a POC is you start isolating people who are just tire kickers versus serious buyers. It becomes a lead qualification mechanism. If you didn't have that, you're going to attract all of these curious buyers who are just curious about AI. They just want to see if it works or not. They will say, "Yes, I'll engage with the POC." They will take 30, 60, 90 days with you. They will burn a lot of resources, never buy. You've just wasted your time. Time is of the essence. So having a price tag to your POC actually indicates that there is seriousness on both sides, so you should charge. (00:33:48): But how do you actually charge for it? You need to charge for it smartly. What this means is that you need to make sure that your POC pricing is not a reflection of your actual commercial deal. Because let's say if you just say it's a 10K POC for a 30-day pilot. If you don't talk about the fact that it is not the same as your commercial discussion, you have now set an anchor that, okay, it's 120K per year kind of deal if the POC works. So you have to be clear that the 10K is only for building a business case. Commercial discussions will follow after that. It is not an indication of the actual commercial discussion. (00:34:28): But your buyer on the other side might still push you saying, "That's all great, but I need a price or a budget, otherwise I won't move forward with it." So there are two ways to actually deflect those kind of questions. The first way is contextualize the price on the value. So you can say something like, if you're pushed for price, "Hey, for customers such as yours, we have been able to at least unlock 10 million in very similar situations. And our pricing is... One is to 10X when it comes to ROI." (00:34:58): So you basically said that you're a million dollars to actually get started, but you actually didn't say it. You just said, "It's a 10 million, and I'm taking one in 10 in exchange for it." So you've given the buyer an indication, but you've framed it in such a manner that actually is justifiable, right? A one in 10X ROI. So that's one way to do it. (00:35:16): They might still say, "Yeah, that's good, but I need a budget." So then rather than just give them a budget saying, "It could be a 200K option," don't do that. That's the worst thing you can actually say. Give them a range. You can say something like, "Look, the final pricing would be anywhere from 500K to a million. And based on the business case that we would co-create with you, we can pick a point in that range that justifies the value that we bring to the table." So you're giving budgetary ranges, right? So that's the other way to actually go about POCs. (00:35:46): So how you navigate your early wins, who you choose is very critical when you're building companies at scale and fast in AI because that actually dictates the destiny for the rest of your future. And picking those early wins is very, very critical. And having buyers who are serious, lead qualifying, having the right POC process, and thinking about POCs as, frankly, not just trying to see if your product actually works and delivers value, but it's a great chance to have a commercial test-and-learn experiment and have fun with it and try to see what you can bring to the table in terms of your value and what portion can you actually take.
turns.zh: 所以 POC，当我们谈论 POC 时，许多创始人将 POC 视为技术功能的证明，以及他们的产品是否在客户环境中实际运行。他们设定了我们所说的期望，“嘿，我们将推出该产品，我们将看看它是否真的有效。”他们可能会说：“我应该对 POC 收费还是不收费？”我们稍后会解开这个问题，无论你是否应该。 (00:32:10)：这实际上是一种完全错误的构建方式。 POC 的框架应该是 POC 的整个目标是创建一个业务案例，句号。它并不是为了证明产品功能适合您的客户环境的集成能力。所有这些都是商业案例的结果。 (00:32:30)：因此，如果您这样构建，您可以说：“看，这是一个为期 30 天的试点，旨在与用户共同创建投资回报率模型并构建业务案例。如果我们在 30 天结束时根据业务案例看到价值，我们就可以进行商业讨论。”这样你实际上就没有谈论你的价格。您只需专注于与客户共同创建业务案例。根据商业案例，您实际上可以制定适当的商业协​​议。如果他们看到价值，他们就会付钱给你。所以以这种方式思考 POC。 (00:33:03)：我经常被问到的问题是：“我应该对 POC 收费吗？”答案是肯定的，但是要聪明。我们来谈谈为什么充电很重要。您需要对 POC 收费的原因是您开始将那些只是轮胎踢脚者和认真的买家隔离开来。它成为一种领先资格机制。如果你没有这个，你就会吸引所有这些对人工智能感兴趣的好奇买家。他们只是想看看它是否有效。他们会说：“是的，我会与 POC 合作。”他们将与您一起度过 30 天、60 天、90 天。他们会消耗大量资源，从不购买。你只是浪费了时间。时间至关重要。因此，你的 POC 上有价格标签实际上表明双方都很认真，所以你应该收费。 (00:33:48)：但实际上如何收费呢？你需要巧妙地收费。这意味着您需要确保您的 POC 定价不反映您的实际商业交易。因为假设您只是说这是一个为期 30 天的试点的 10K POC。如果你不谈论它与你的商业讨论不一样的事实，那么你现在已经设定了一个锚点，好吧，如果 POC 有效的话，每年的交易额是 12 万美元。所以你必须清楚，10K 仅用于构建业务案例。此后将进行商业讨论。这并不代表实际的商业讨论。 (00:34:28)：但另一边的买家可能仍然会催促你说：“这很好，但我需要一个价格或预算，否则我不会继续这样做。”因此，有两种方法可以真正转移此类问题。第一种方法是将价格与价值结合起来。因此，如果您被要求价格，您可以这样说：“嘿，对于像您这样的客户，我们已经能够在非常相似的情况下至少解锁 1000 万个。我们的定价是……就投资回报率而言，是 10 倍。” (00:34:58)：所以你基本上说你需要一百万美元才能真正开始，但你实际上没有说出来。你就说，一千万，我拿十分之一换。所以你已经给了买家一个指示，但你是以一种实际上合理的方式来构建它的，对吗？投资回报率十分之一。这是一种方法。 (00:35:16)：他们可能仍然会说，“是的，那很好，但我需要预算。”因此，不要只给他们一个预算，说“这可能是一个 20 万的选择”，不要这样做。这是你实际上可以说的最糟糕的话。给他们一个范围。您可以这样说：“看，最终定价从 50 万到 100 万不等。根据我们与您共同创建的业务案例，我们可以在该范围内选择一个点，以证明我们带来的价值是合理的。”所以你给出了预算范围，对吧？这就是实际进行 POC 的另一种方式。 (00:35:46)：因此，当您在人工智能领域快速大规模创建公司时，如何驾驭早期胜利以及选择谁非常关键，因为这实际上决定了您未来的命运。选择那些早期的胜利是非常非常关键的。拥有认真的买家，引导资格，拥有正确的 POC 流程，坦率地说，将 POC 视为不仅仅是想看看你的产品是否真正有效并提供价值，而且这是一个进行商业测试和学习实验的好机会，并从中获得乐趣，并尝试看看你可以带来什么价值以及你实际上可以拿走多少部分。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: So when you talk about AI companies and monetization models, we get asked this question. "Should I be usage-based? Should I be outcome? Should I be a copilot mode? Or how do I actually think about my pricing model?" So we came up with this framework, which is a relatively simple, straightforward framework, but very powerful. (00:39:39): So there are two axes here. One is attribution, and the other one is autonomy. And when you have high attribution and high autonomy, that is when you have high pricing power, and we'll come back to that in a bit, right? (00:39:51): So let's take the first bottom-left quadrant. That is the quadrant where your attribution is low and your autonomy is low. In that situation, the best pricing archetype that actually fits is it is actually a seed-based or a subscription model because there's not much to do about it because you're not being able to attribute a lot of value to what you bring, but you're in a copilot mode and you're not in an autonomous mode, so a seed-based pricing would actually make sense. (00:40:18): But if you're at that quadrant, the immediate thing to think about is, how do you actually build more attribution and move to the right so that you actually get more pricing power? So if you think about the bottom-right quadrant, those are companies that have actually done that. They can prove more attribution to what they actually bring to the table, but they are still not in a fully autonomous mode, as in there is still humans in the loop. (00:40:43): If you take Cursor, for instance, it definitely improves productivity, can actually bring down the time to actually do code, the attribution is clear, but it's still in a copilot mode. In those kind of situations, a hybrid pricing model is the best option where you still have a seed-based model for the copilot kind of use case, but you also layer in a consumption model which actually says there are a certain number of AI credits or tokens that can layer in the usage aspects. So if you use more and more, then you're actually paying more on consumption. So it's a hybrid model that actually works there. (00:41:18): If you look at the top-left quadrant, those are products that are very autonomous but are not strong on attribution. So these tend to be mostly backend or infrastructure kind of products that are core critical to run businesses, can be autonomous, but they're not directly impacting the KPIs that businesses are tracking, and hence cannot prove attribution very effectively. So in that situation, you need to be on a pay-for-what-you-consume and a usage-based model. A seed-based model would not make sense because it's autonomous. There's no human in the loop. But that's why you're also in a usage-based model, saying the more you use it, the more you're actually charged. And usage becomes a proxy for the value that you bring to the table. (00:42:07): The quadrant that you really want to be in is the golden quadrant, which is the top-right one. That's the outcome-based pricing model where you have great autonomy and great attribution. And here is where I think AI can be really magical. So this means you're not only charging for work delivered, but you're charging for work delivered that was delivered by AI without no humans in the loop. So that becomes more of an outcome-based model situation. (00:42:35): So a classic example here is Intercom for Fin. What they actually do is they charge based on an AI resolution. So if an AI is able to resolve the ticket completely independently without a human in the loop, then they charge for it. If a human intervention is needed, they don't charge for it. So they're more on an outcome-based model. Or companies like Charge Flow would charge up to 25% on a charge bag that they're able to actually recover, because these are core savings that you actually bring to the table based on your AI. It is highly attributable, highly autonomous so you can start moving towards an outcome-based pricing model. (00:43:14): If you look at the state of where AI is today, as of the day of recording this podcast, now, the most popular model is right now a hybrid pricing model. So because this is also expected, because the previous SaaS playbook was usually on the seat-based model, but they've all now moved on to at least a hybrid to actually incorporate AI credits and usage, et cetera, about 5% of companies are probably in a true outcome-based pricing model as of today. But those companies, some of the best ones are able to recover 25 to 50% of the value that they actually bring to the table. (00:43:54): In the classic SaaS situation, we used to say if you can charge 10 to 20% of the value, that's actually great. But in AI, you can actually charge 25 to 50% because it is autonomous, you're doing it with the AI. There's no humans in the loop. You are creating incremental value to the business metrics. You are producing hard-cost savings. There's opportunity costs. You can justify all of that. It's attributable. So you can actually take 25 to 50% of what you bring to the table. (00:44:22): In a lot of benchmarks and studies that actually show, and this is also my belief, that in the next three years that 5% number will move to 25%. So what this really means is if you want to win in AI, figure out a way to get to that quadrant because that's a magic quadrant. If you can truly price based on outcomes, you've achieved and unlock tremendous value.
turns.zh: 因此，当你谈论人工智能公司和货币化模式时，我们会被问到这个问题。 “我应该基于使用情况吗？我应该以结果为基础吗？我应该成为副驾驶模式吗？或者我实际上如何考虑我的定价模型？”所以我们想出了这个框架，这是一个相对简单、直接的框架，但是非常强大。 (00:39:39)：所以这里有两个轴。一是归因，二是自主。当你拥有高归因和高自主权时，那就是你拥有高定价能力的时候，我们稍后会回到这一点，对吗？ (00:39:51)：让我们看第一个左下象限。那是你的归因低、自主权低的象限。在这种情况下，真正适合的最佳定价原型是它实际上是基于种子的或订阅模型，因为对此没有太多可做的，因为你无法为你带来的东西赋予很多价值，但你处于副驾驶模式而不是自主模式，所以基于种子的定价实际上是有意义的。 (00:40:18)：但如果你处于那个象限，首先要考虑的是，如何真正建立更多归因并向右移动，以便真正获得更多定价权？因此，如果你考虑一下右下象限，那些公司实际上已经做到了这一点。他们可以证明更多的归因于他们实际带来的东西，但他们仍然没有处于完全自主的模式，因为仍然有人类在循环中。 (00:40:43)：如果以 Cursor 为例，它肯定会提高生产力，实际上可以减少实际编写代码的时间，归因很明确，但它仍然处于副驾驶模式。在这种情况下，混合定价模型是最好的选择，你仍然有一个基于种子的模型用于副驾驶类型的用例，但你也可以分层消费模型，该模型实际上表示有一定数量的人工智能积分或代币可以在使用方面分层。因此，如果您使用得越来越多，那么您实际上在消费上付出了更多的代价。所以这是一个实际可行的混合模型。 (00:41:18)：如果你看一下左上象限，就会发现这些产品非常自主，但归因能力不强。因此，这些产品往往大多是后端或基础设施类型的产品，对企业运营至关重要，可以是自主的，但它们不会直接影响企业跟踪的 KPI，因此无法非常有效地证明归因。因此，在这种情况下，您需要采用按需付费和基于使用的模型。基于种子的模型没有意义，因为它是自主的。循环中没有人。但这就是为什么您也采用基于使用情况的模型，即您使用的次数越多，实际收取的费用就越多。使用情况成为您带来的价值的代理。 (00:42:07)：您真正想要进入的象限是黄金象限，即右上角的象限。这就是基于结果的定价模型，您拥有很大的自主权和很大的归因权。我认为这就是人工智能真正神奇的地方。因此，这意味着您不仅要对交付的工作收费，还要对人工智能在没有人工介入的情况下交付的工作收费。因此，这更像是一种基于结果的模型情况。 (00:42:35)：一个典型的例子是 Fin 的 Intercom。他们实际上所做的是根据人工智能分辨率进行收费。因此，如果人工智能能够在没有人类参与的情况下完全独立地解决问题，那么他们就会收费。如果需要人工干预，他们不会收费。所以他们更多地采用基于结果的模型。或者像 Charge Flow 这样的公司会对他们能够实际回收的费用包收取高达 25% 的费用，因为这些是你根据 AI 实际带来的核心节省。它具有高度可归因性、高度自主性，因此您可以开始转向基于结果的定价模型。 (00:43:14)：如果你看看人工智能今天的状况，截至录制本播客之日，现在最流行的模型是混合定价模型。因为这也是预料之中的，因为之前的 SaaS 剧本通常采用基于席位的模型，但现在他们都已经转向至少一种混合型，以实际纳入人工智能积分和使用等，所以截至今天，大约 5% 的公司可能采用真正的基于结果的定价模型。但这些公司，其中一些最好的公司能够收回他们实际带来的价值的 25% 到 50%。 (00:43:54)：在经典的 SaaS 情况下，我们过去常常说，如果你能收取价值的 10% 到 20%，那实际上就很好了。但在人工智能中，你实际上可以收取 25% 到 50% 的费用，因为它是自主的，你是用人工智能来做的。循环中没有人类。您正在为业务指标创造增量价值。您正在节省硬成本。有机会成本。你可以证明这一切都是合理的。这是可归因的。所以你实际上可以拿走你所带来的25%到50%。 (00:44:22)：许多基准测试和研究实际上表明，这也是我的信念，在未来三年内，5% 的数字将上升至 25%。所以这真正的意思是，如果你想在人工智能领域获胜，就想办法到达那个象限，因为那是一个神奇的象限。如果您能够真正根据结果定价，您就已经实现并释放了巨大的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay. I'm just going to pause again. This is amazing. Madhavan, thank you so much for it. I love, again, that you just spent years, decades studying this stuff, come here, tell us all the answers of what we should be doing. This is incredible. (00:45:01): Let me ask you this. By the way, for folks not watching on YouTube, the companies you have in the golden quadrant, outcome-based pricing, Sierra, Fin, and Chargeflow. We've got the founder of Sierra and Fin coming on the podcast soon, so we'll talk about all this with those guys.
turns.zh: 哇。好的。我要再次暂停。这太棒了。马达万，非常感谢你。我再次喜欢你花了几年、几十年的时间研究这些东西，来到这里，告诉我们我们应该做什么的所有答案。这太不可思议了。 (00:45:01)：让我问你这个问题。顺便说一句，对于那些没有在 YouTube 上观看的人来说，您可以了解位于黄金象限、基于结果的定价、Sierra、Fin 和 Chargeflow 中的公司。 Sierra 和 Fin 的创始人很快就会出现在播客中，所以我们将与这些人讨论所有这些。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 惊人的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So is the way to use this two-by-two figuring out your model? Is it like, "Okay, I'm like Cursor. I'm going to go in this quadrant," or is it, "How do I get to outcome-based no matter what? That's where I need to be"?
turns.zh: 那么使用这个二乘二的方法来计算你的模型吗？是不是“好吧，我就像 Cursor。我要进入这个象限”，还是“无论如何我怎样才能做到以结果为基础？这就是我需要的地方”？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Yeah, so that's a great question. The first one is to actually figure out what is your right archetype based on where you are today. I think that is most important. If you try to rush into an outcome-based pricing model but cannot prove attribution, you will fail. So it is really coming up with what is the right archetype based on what I'm doing today, but also use this two-by-two to say, "How do I paint a vision to actually get to outcome based? And can I get close to that? Or can I be purely an outcome-based model? How do I evolve into that?" (00:46:05): What that would mean is, how do I build functionality in the products to actually show attribution, how do I build more agentic workforces to take the human out of the loop and be more autonomous, and being thoughtful about your vision and strategy so that you will orient yourself towards more outcome-based pricing models. So when you think about increasing attribution, that means, first of all, understanding what are the KPIs of your customers. How do they track their business performance? Can you impact it? Can you productize things in your product that showcase that you are actually affecting those KPIs in a positive manner? Can you build dashboards to show value attribution? Can you do those value audits that we talked about on an ongoing basis to actually show that you're bringing a lot of value to the table and is attributable to you? So how do you create these kind of attribution mechanisms become important and also autonomous based on building more agentic workforces that can actually be on an autonomous mold? (00:47:04): So pick the right archetype and plan to get to as close as you can to the outcome-based pricing model. That's how I would use the two-by-two. And you actually kind of see this happening with certain industries, right? If you think about coding as a overall category... Like back in the day with GitHub, everyone, they started with a seed-based model. They've now moved to the hybrid-based pricing model with Cursors and everyone else, but the natural move would be more towards a outcome-based pricing model where a AI agent can probably code everything at the same time, debug it, and you're kind of almost hiring a AI developer or AI QA person. And that actually becomes more closer to a outcome-based model because it's attributable and autonomous. So that is picking the right archetype and then figuring out your pathway is the key way to interpret this two-by-two.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一个很好的问题。第一个是根据你今天的处境真正找出你正确的原型是什么。我认为这是最重要的。如果你试图仓促采用基于结果的定价模型但无法证明归因，你就会失败。因此，它实际上是根据我今天所做的事情提出什么是正确的原型，但也用这个二乘二来说，“我如何描绘一个愿景，以真正实现基于结果？我可以接近它吗？或者我可以纯粹是一个基于结果的模型吗？我如何演变为那个？” (00:46:05)：这意味着，我如何在产品中构建功能以实际显示归因，如何建立更具代理性的员工队伍以将人带出循环并变得更加自主，并深思熟虑您的愿景和策略，以便您将自己定位于更加基于结果的定价模型。因此，当您考虑增加归因时，这意味着首先要了解客户的 KPI 是什么。他们如何跟踪他们的业务绩效？你能影响它吗？您能否将产品中的内容产品化，以展示您实际上正在以积极的方式影响这些 KPI？您可以构建仪表板来显示价值归因吗？您能否持续进行我们讨论的那些价值审核，以实际表明您正在为桌面带来很多价值并且归功于您？那么，如何在建立更多能够真正采用自主模式的代理劳动力的基础上，创建这种既重要又自主的归因机制呢？ (00:47:04)：因此，选择正确的原型并计划尽可能接近基于结果的定价模型。这就是我使用二乘二的方式。您实际上看到某些行业正在发生这种情况，对吧？如果你将编码视为一个整体类别……就像当年的 GitHub 一样，每个人都是从基于种子的模型开始的。他们现在已经转向使用 Cursors 和其他所有人的基于混合的定价模型，但自然的转变将更多地转向基于结果的定价模型，在这种模型中，人工智能代理可能可以同时对所有内容进行编码、调试，而你几乎是在雇用人工智能开发人员或人工智能 QA 人员。这实际上变得更接近基于结果的模型，因为它是可归因的和自主的。因此，选择正确的原型，然后弄清楚你的路径是解释这个二乘二的关键方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This explains why everyone's pulling agents. That's where the money's at, what you're telling us here.
turns.zh: 这就解释了为什么每个人都是拉动代理。这就是钱的所在，你在这里告诉我们的。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Yeah. It's going to be the age of The Matrix. Too many agents.
turns.zh: 是的。这将是《黑客帝国》的时代。代理太多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Agent Smiths everywhere. They didn't turn out too great. So what I'm hearing is if I were Canva... So Canva here in your model is bottom right. They're in a hybrid pricing model. They have a base fee and consumption fee. What you would do if you were helping Canva is what can you build that creates more autonomy, an autonomous version of Canva? And it's not like you need to do this. It's just you have more pricing power if you figure something out there.
turns.zh: 史密斯特工无处不在。结果并没有太好。所以我听到的是如果我是 Canva...所以 Canva 在你的模型中位于右下角。他们采用混合定价模式。他们有基本费和消费费。如果你帮助 Canva，你会做什么，你可以构建什么来创造更多的自主权，即 Canva 的自主版本？而且你不需要这样做。只是如果你弄清楚了一些事情，你就有了更大的定价权。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Exactly. And a good case for that is the Fin product from Intercom. Because traditionally, all of those kind of companies used to price based on an agent basis. How many customer service agents are actually using the product? It used to be seed based, but they built out Fin, which is a completely AI resolution for those kind of support tickets. And then that actually enables them to move to the outcome-based pricing model quadrant.
turns.zh: 确切地。 Intercom 的 Fin 产品就是一个很好的例子。因为传统上，所有这些类型的公司都过去根据代理定价。有多少客户服务代理实际使用该产品？它曾经是基于种子的，但他们构建了 Fin，这是针对此类支持票证的完全人工智能解决方案。然后，这实际上使他们能够转向基于结果的定价模型象限。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So say you're an AI founder today. You're thinking about your pricing strategy, your monetization strategy long term. Your advice is work with design partners, create these POCs where you work on this ROI model with them to ideally find some outcome-based pricing strategy. Is that a good way to summarize it? What would you add to that?
turns.zh: 惊人的。假设您今天是一名人工智能创始人。你正在考虑你的定价策略，你的长期盈利策略。您的建议是与设计合作伙伴合作，创建这些 POC，与他们一起研究投资回报率模型，以理想地找到一些基于结果的定价策略。这是一个很好的总结方式吗？你会添加什么？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Yes. I mean, at least be able to contextualize the business case. Even if you're not moving to an outcome-based pricing model, be clear on the outcome that you're actually creating for your customers through that business case, which actually will enable you to charge a fair price in exchange for that outcome. And if your customers agree with the business case, then you can actually take a portion of that.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，至少能够将业务案例置于情境中。即使您不打算采用基于结果的定价模型，也要清楚您通过该业务案例实际为客户创建的结果，这实际上将使您能够收取公平的价格来换取该结果。如果您的客户同意该业务案例，那么您实际上可以从中获得一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fin, actually, they're a new sponsor of the podcast, and I learned... I didn't know this. It costs 99 cents for every support ticket they solve [inaudible 00:49:51].
turns.zh: 芬，实际上，他们是播客的新赞助商，我了解到……我不知道这一点。他们解决的每张支持请求的费用为 99 美分 [听不清 00:49:51]。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Through AI.
turns.zh: 通过人工智能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Through AI.
turns.zh: 通过人工智能。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Exactly. If it needs a human intervention, then they don't charge for it.
turns.zh: 确切地。如果需要人工干预，那么他们不会收费。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And it's just like, what? That's such a simple story. Your agent costs 20 bucks. This thing costs 99 cents
turns.zh: 是的。就像，什么？这是一个多么简单的故事。你的代理费用是20美元。这东西要99美分

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Yeah. That is two chapters in one beautifully simple pricing and an outcome-based pricing model.
turns.zh: 是的。这是一个非常简单的定价和基于结果的定价模型的两章。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And interestingly, they were the most hated pricing model initially. I did a survey on Twitter ones, like, "What products do you pay the most for?" and it was always Intercom. And everyone hated their pricing, and they found a solution.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，它们最初是最令人讨厌的定价模式。我在 Twitter 上做了一项调查，比如“你为哪些产品支付最多的钱？”而且总是对讲机。每个人都讨厌他们的定价，他们找到了解决方案。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: I think they found a great solution.
turns.zh: 我认为他们找到了一个很好的解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So is there anything else along these lines that you think companies, especially AI companies, should be thinking when they're thinking about pricing that you'd want to share before we move on to other stuff?
turns.zh: 好的。那么，您认为公司，尤其是人工智能公司，在考虑定价时还应该考虑什么，在我们继续讨论其他问题之前，您希望分享一下这些内容吗？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: I think we've covered most of the topics. Like we said, it's being thoughtful about POCs, choosing the right pricing archetype or the pricing models. Those things become very critical in the early stages. But when you start scaling and, let's say, you become a multi-product company, then you need to start focusing on, "What kind of packaging strategy should I have? Is it a platform plus add-ons? Should I have versions of the products like good, better, best? Should I tackle different use cases because now my AI can solve an insurance use case and a healthcare use case? Should I productize to different use cases? Is that my packaging strategy? Or should I keep it completely modularized for people to pick and choose?" (00:51:17): So these kind of questions become more critical, and that's why the chapter on blowing up your packaging from your early days and coming up with your packaging strategy for your scale-up phase become very critical. So I think that's the next thing that founders would be hit with, as in when they build multiple products, they need to think about the whole packaging, cross-selling, up-selling motion.
turns.zh: 我想我们已经涵盖了大部分主题。正如我们所说，要考虑 POC，选择正确的定价原型或定价模型。这些事情在早期阶段变得非常关键。但是，当你开始扩展，假设你成为一家多产品公司，那么你需要开始关注，“我应该有什么样的包装策略？它是一个平台加附加组件吗？我应该有好、更好、最好之类的产品版本吗？我应该处理不同的用例，因为现在我的人工智能可以解决保险用例和医疗保健用例吗？我应该产品化到不同的用例吗？这是我的包装策略吗？或者我应该保持它完全模块化，以供人们选择？” (00:51:17)：所以这类问题变得更加关键，这就是为什么关于从早期开始炸毁包装并为放大阶段制定包装策略的章节变得非常重要。所以我认为这是创始人接下来会遇到的问题，因为当他们构建多种产品时，他们需要考虑整个包装、交叉销售、追加销售动作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on something I was about to ask, which is a change in your pricing strategy. How often is it a success to change the way you price? I know we're talking about you need to get it right from the beginning if you're an AI company. In your experience, how often... What does it take to successfully shift the way you price down the road if people are listening to this and are like, "Shit, we already have this pricing strategy"?
turns.zh: 这涉及到我想问的问题，即你们定价策略的改变。改变定价方式的成功率有多少？我知道我们正在讨论的是，如果你是一家人工智能公司，你需要从一开始就把事情做好。根据您的经验，如果人们听到这个并说“糟糕，我们已经有了这个定价策略”，那么如何才能成功地改变您的定价方式呢？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Back in the day, we used to say that you should revisit your pricing strategy, overall pricing model, how much you're charging at least once in two years. With AI, that's probably reduced in half because of the scale with which and the speed with which companies are built and competing. (00:52:16): So I would say that it is an ongoing journey. It is not like you just solve it in day one, fill it, and forget it. You have to be thoughtful from day one, but also be ready to pivot, iterate, and you're going to learn along your journey. So the whole point is to think about pricing as also a test-and-learn opportunity in your early days. (00:52:38): And there are things that you would change more often, and there are things that you probably don't want to change too often. Things like pricing model, unless you really changed your attribution autonomy, there is no need to shift your pricing model. Stay within that archetype. Don't confuse things. (00:52:54): But there are things like price points. Should I increase my price because it's been six months a year? Yeah, you should. Because in a year there's probably prices go up three to 5% for everything that you consume. But how can you actually increase your prices and be thoughtful about it? So that entire chapter on how to do price increases smartly become very important in the scale-up phase. (00:53:16): I think Warren Buffett summarized this really well. He said the true definition of a company is a pricing power. And if you have a prayer session for doing a 10% price increase, you have a terrible business. So you have to be able to increase prices over a bit of time. But how do you do it strategically that does not affect too much churn, but you're also able to pass on the increase as a value exchange, those things become critical.
turns.zh: 过去，我们曾经说过，您应该重新审视您的定价策略、整体定价模型、每两年至少一次收取的费用。有了人工智能，由于公司建立和竞争的规模和速度，这一数字可能会减少一半。 (00:52:16)：所以我想说这是一个持续的旅程。这并不是说你只是在第一天解决它，填充它，然后忘记它。你必须从第一天起就深思熟虑，但也要做好调整、迭代的准备，并且你将在你的旅程中不断学习。因此，重点是将定价视为早期的测试和学习机会。 (00:52:38)：有些事情你会更频繁地改变，有些事情你可能不想经常改变。像定价模型这样的事情，除非你真的改变了你的归因自主权，否则没有必要改变你的定价模型。留在那个原型内。别把事情搞混了。 (00:52:54)：但是还有价格点之类的东西。因为一年已经过去六个月了，我应该提高价格吗？是的，你应该。因为一年内你消费的所有东西的价格可能会上涨 3% 到 5%。但如何才能真正提高价格并深思熟虑呢？因此，关于如何巧妙地提高价格的整章在扩大规模阶段变得非常重要。 (00:53:16)：我认为沃伦·巴菲特对此总结得非常好。他说，公司的真正定义是定价权。如果你为价格上涨 10% 举行祈祷会，那么你的生意就会很糟糕。所以你必须能够在一段时间内提高价格。但是，如何从战略上做到这一点，既不会影响太多客户流失，又能够将增长作为价值交换来传递，这些事情变得至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Zooming out a little bit, something that I love about your book is you structured it around these axioms. You have a bunch of these really clever axioms that get stuck in your head and help you think about pricing. Can you share some of your favorites, maybe two or three referred axioms from the book?
turns.zh: 惊人的。缩小一点，我喜欢你的书的一点是你围绕这些公理构建了它。你有一堆非常聪明的公理，它们会深深地印在你的脑海里，帮助你思考定价。你能分享一些你最喜欢的，也许是书中提到的两三个公理吗？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: You talked about Sierra being in your park founders. I don't know if that's Clay, but here's a shout-out for Clay. So Clay actually read the entire book and gave me feedback, Scaling Innovation, the similar copy that he actually had. I called it Scaling Innovation Axioms throughout the book. And the whole point of the axioms was that at the end of the day, if you can just take all the axioms, put it in a printout next to your desk is the summary of the book. And it's like PT statements that you'll just remember what to do. (00:54:26): So he came up with this idea that, "Hey, rather than calling them just generic scaling innovation axioms, you need to brand each and every axiom." And I thought that was a brilliant idea. So I went about coming up with a unique... He even contributed to some of the names. We came up with some unique names for each axiom. (00:54:45): And here's the other fun fact. Probably I'm geeking out too much. But when I counted the number of axioms, there were 42 axioms. And I didn't try to make this up. And if you're a Hitchhiker's fan, then you know that's the answer to everything. (00:54:58): But jokes apart, let me unpack a few axioms. One of my first favorite axioms, what I call is the 20-80 axiom. Especially in tech companies, 20% of what you build drives 80% of the willingness to pay. But the irony is that the 20% is the easiest thing to build often. So what founders do is they take this 20%, build it, put it out in the market almost for free, and then they're chasing their tails to build 80% stuff that's only driving 20% willingness to pay. So if you have not been thoughtful about that, you've given the farm away unintentionally. (00:55:37): So truly understanding what drives willingness to pay in your product is critical. And I think people call it the MVP. I think we should change the definition of MVP. It shouldn't be minimum viable product, it should be the most valuable product. And be thoughtful about what are you actually giving out as your early products I think is key. That's the 20-80 axiom. (00:55:58): Probably my second one is the price paralysis axioms. So what that means is your reluctance to do a price increase is often internal and emotional and it's not external and logical. This goes back to the same prayer session to actually do a price increase. If you're holding hands, you have a terrible business. So it's mostly internal and emotional, and how do you be thoughtful about price increases become important. (00:56:29): Probably my third favorite one is stopping churn before it happens, so stopping churn axiom. So to stop churn, you need to attract customers who won't leave. That sounds counterintuitive, but that's the best way to actually stop churn. What does this actually mean? Most companies will try to stop churn when someone actually says, "I want to go." It is too late, and you're being reactive. At the most, you'll throw some offers. They will stay for another six months, and they will leave. They've already made that determination. (00:56:59): The way to stop churn is to start acquiring customers who won't leave. And that is the most important thing. So if you look back at your data and say, "Who are the types of customers who actually tend to stay longer? What are their characteristics? How can I focus my acquisition dollars in getting more of those?" then you stop churn before it happens. And that's the key.
turns.zh: 你谈到塞拉是你的公园创始人之一。我不知道那是不是克莱，但这里是对克莱的大声喊叫。所以克莱实际上读了整本书并向我提供了反馈，《扩展创新》，这是他实际拥有的类似副本。我在整本书中将其称为“扩展创新公理”。这些公理的全部要点是，在一天结束时，如果你能把所有的公理都拿出来，把它打印出来放在你桌子旁边，那就是这本书的摘要。这就像 PT 语句一样，你只会记住要做什么。 (00:54:26)：所以他提出了这个想法，“嘿，你需要给每一个公理打上品牌，而不是仅仅称它们为通用的规模创新公理。”我认为这是一个绝妙的主意。所以我开始想出一个独特的……他甚至还贡献了一些名字。我们为每个公理想出了一些独特的名称。 (00:54:45)：这是另一个有趣的事实。可能是我太迷恋了。但当我数一下公理数量时，有42条公理。我并没有试图弥补这一点。如果您是《搭便车》的粉丝，那么您就会知道这就是一切的答案。 (00:54:58)：不过开玩笑之余，让我来解开一些公理。我最喜欢的公理之一，我称之为 20-80 公理。尤其是在科技公司，你所构建的 20% 的产品会驱动 80% 的支付意愿。但讽刺的是，20% 往往是最容易构建的。所以创始人所做的就是拿这 20% 进行构建，几乎免费地将其投放到市场，然后他们追逐自己的尾巴构建 80% 的东西，而这些东西只能推动 20% 的人愿意付费。所以，如果你没有考虑到这一点，你就无意中放弃了农场。 (00:55:37)：因此，真正了解是什么推动了产品的支付意愿至关重要。我认为人们称之为 MVP。我认为我们应该改变 MVP 的定义。它不应该是最低可行的产品，而应该是最有价值的产品。并考虑一下你实际上提供了什么，因为我认为你的早期产品是关键。这就是 20-80 公理。 (00:55:58)：我的第二个可能是价格瘫痪公理。因此，这意味着您不愿意涨价通常是出于内心和情感，而不是外在和逻辑。这又回到了同一个祈祷会，以实际提高价格。如果你们手牵着手，那你们的生意就很糟糕了。因此，这主要是内部和情感上的，如何考虑价格上涨变得很重要。 (00:56:29)：我最喜欢的第三个可能是在流失发生之前停止流失，所以停止流失公理。因此，为了阻止客户流失，您需要吸引那些不会离开的客户。这听起来有悖常理，但这是真正阻止客户流失的最佳方法。这实际上意味着什么？当有人真正说“我想走”时，大多数公司都会试图阻止客户流失。已经太晚了，而且你正在做出反应。最多，你会提出一些报价。他们将再呆六个月，然后他们就会离开。他们已经做出了这个决定。 (00:56:59)：停止流失的方法是开始获取不会离开的客户。这是最重要的事情。因此，如果你回顾一下你的数据并说：“哪些类型的客户实际上倾向于停留更长时间？他们有什么特征？我如何才能集中我的收购资金来获得更多这样的客户？”然后你就可以在流失发生之前停止流失。这就是关键。

turns.zh: 所以实际上就是所有这些。市场份额、钱包份额、收购、货币化、保留都是相关的。你不能孤立地思考它们。所以我不会只说对于钱包共享你需要做什么。如果您想同时增加市场份额和钱包份额……比方说，您需要制定正确的土地扩张策略。土地可以帮助您收购。该扩展可以帮助您共享钱包。 (00:59:54)：如果你有一个定价模型，那么你需要有一个可以让你更快获取的定价模型，因为它很直观，但它也应该帮助你恢复价值，就像你的货币化一样。如果人们了解你的定价模式，他们实际上就会留下来。所以这一切都是齐头并进的。所以我不会孤立地以一种或另一种方式思考。这就是为什么这九种策略实际上非常强大。因为如果你遵循这些策略，你就不会陷入单引擎困境。这些都是经过尝试和测试的策略，说明如何以深思熟虑并同等重视市场份额和钱包份额的方式建立业务。
